claims.claim: The energy in the sunlight on your skin spent more than a hundred thousand years getting out of the Sun.
claims.source_checked: Mitalas & Sills, ApJ 401, 759-760 (1992), NASA ADS scan (both pages read); Crossref record for doi:10.1086/172103; NASA MSFC 'The Solar Interior' (solarscience.msfc.nasa.gov/interior.shtml); NASA SVS 11084; Crossref record for Stix doi:10.1023/A:1022952621810
claims.note: MS92 abstract and section 3: t_d = 1.7 x 10^5 yr for a photon diffusing from the centre to the inner edge of the convective zone; they state the convective crossing time is 'very much shorter', so the total exit time is still > 1e5 yr. Their Fig. 2 also puts the diffusion time from ~0.25 R (edge of the core) to the convection zone at roughly 1.2e5 yr (figure reading), so energy released anywhere in the core still takes > 1e5 yr. MSFC: the energy is carried by photons through the radiative zone and 'an individual photon takes about a million years to finally reach the interface layer' (~1e6). SVS's '40,000 years' contradicts the lower bound, but the disagreement is recorded in SOURCES with a reason (MS92 is peer-reviewed and shows the common 0.5-1.0 cm step gives 3e3-3e4 yr, 'much too short'), which meets A3. 'More than a hundred thousand' is a lower bound under 1.7e5, not a rounding up. Saying 'energy' rather than 'a photon' matches MSFC's framing (energy carried by photons that bounce particle to particle). Stix 2003 not read at source (bibliographic details match Crossref: Solar Physics 212, 3-6, 2003); the hook does not rest on it and SOURCES says so (A2).

claims.claim: The trip from the Sun to you took eight minutes.
claims.source_checked: NIST CODATA 2022 c (physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Value?c); NASA SVS 11084; NSSDC Earth Fact Sheet (cross-check of AU and eccentricity; IAU 2012 B2 itself not reachable)
claims.note: c = 299,792,458 m/s exact (CODATA 2022, read). 149,597,870,700 m / c = 499.0 s = 8 min 19 s. NSSDC gives semimajor axis 149.598e6 km, perihelion 147.095e6 km, aphelion 152.100e6 km, e = 0.0167, so the trip is 8.18-8.46 min (SOURCES' 8.2-8.5 min and +/-1.7% are right). SVS, cited in SOURCES entry 5, states 'Light takes eight minutes to travel the 93 million miles from the sun to Earth', the same rounding. The IAU resolution page was not reachable; the AU value was checked against NSSDC instead. Optional: also cite SVS in SOURCES entry 1.

claims.claim: Getting out was the slow part.
claims.source_checked: Derived from claims 1 and 2 (MS92, MSFC, CODATA, SVS)

claims.claim: But it is not the same light.
claims.source_checked: NASA MSFC 'The Solar Interior'; NASA SVS 11084
claims.note: MSFC: inside, the energy moves as radiation that is 'mostly gamma-rays and x-rays' and leaves the surface 'as visible light'; SVS: each photon is 'absorbed by other atoms and emitted repeatedly until reaching the sun's surface'. Both support that the light that leaves is not the light made inside.

claims.claim: Inside, it travels as gamma rays and X-rays.
claims.source_checked: NASA MSFC 'The Solar Interior'; NIST CODATA 2022 Wien wavelength displacement constant (physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Value?bwien)
claims.note: Overstates the source. MSFC says the energy diffuses 'by radiation (mostly gamma-rays and x-rays) through the radiative zone and by convective fluid flows (boiling motion) through the convection zone, the outermost 30%'. 'Inside' with no qualifier covers the convection zone too, where the source says the energy is carried by convection, not as gamma rays or X-rays; 'mostly' is also dropped. Second, a pedant break: gamma rays come from the reactions (MSFC: pp-chain step 2 makes 'a gamma ray'), but the radiation diffusing outward is thermal; with MSFC's temperatures (15 MK centre, 7 MK at 0.25 R, 2 MK at 0.7 R) and Wien's b = 2.897771955e-3 m K (CODATA 2022), its peak is ~6.4, 3.0 and 0.86 keV, all X-ray, far below gamma-ray energies. Change to: 'Deep inside, it travels as X-rays.' and add to SOURCES entry 4 the MSFC radiative/convection split and the Wien calculation. If the owner prefers to keep MSFC's wording, the minimum fix is 'Deep inside, it travels mostly as gamma rays and X-rays.' (scopes it to the radiative zone), with the gamma-ray caveat recorded in SOURCES as a disagreement (A3).

claims.source_checked: NASA MSFC 'The Solar Interior'; NASA SVS 11084
claims.note: MSFC: the reactions release 'the energy that ultimately leaves the surface as visible light'. SVS: photons 'stream out' once at the surface.
> 1e5 years old (1.7e5 per MS92, ~1e6 per MSFC); 'ancient' is a fair description, not a new number.

claims.claim: Its last eight minutes were the trip to you.
claims.source_checked: Rests on claim 2 (CODATA c, SVS 11084, NSSDC cross-check)
claims.note: 8 min 19 s from the photosphere to Earth; SVS: 'Light takes eight minutes to travel ... from the sun to Earth'.

claims.claim: First sentence alone (A4): a viewer who swipes at second two leaves believing the energy in sunlight took over 100,000 years to get out of the Sun.
claims.note: True as stated (see claim 1). It avoids the popular false form ('a photon takes N years to escape'): it talks about energy, and gives a lower bound supported by the peer-reviewed figure. Nothing in the first sentence depends on a later line to be true.

claims.claim: "8 MINUTES" / "surface to your skin" / "not to scale", over the Sun-Earth shot with a pulse crossing the gap
claims.source_checked: NIST CODATA c; NASA SVS 11084; NSSDC Earth Fact Sheet
claims.note: Photosphere to Earth = 8.2-8.5 min; 'surface' is the right start point (MSFC: light leaves the surface). Sizes and distance are labelled not to scale (A6).

claims.claim: "100,000+ YEARS" / "energy, core to surface" / "not to scale"
claims.note: MS92: 1.7e5 yr diffusion from the centre to the convection zone, convective crossing 'very much shorter'; from the core's edge (~0.25 R) Fig. 2 still gives ~1.2e5 yr. MSFC: ~1e6 yr. '100,000+' is a supported lower bound for energy from the core to the surface.

claims.claim: "THE TRIP" / "8 minutes to you" / "not to scale", back on the Sun-Earth shot
claims.note: Same claim as 2; labelled not to scale.

claims.claim: Sun cutaway with rings at 0.25 R and 0.7 R
claims.source_checked: NASA MSFC 'The Solar Interior'; Crossref record for Christensen-Dalsgaard, Gough & Thompson, ApJ 378, 413 (1991)
claims.note: MSFC: core is the innermost 25%; radiative zone from 25% to 70%; convection zone the outermost 30%. The 0.713 R helioseismic value in SOURCES was not read at source (only the Crossref bibliographic record: 'The depth of the solar convection zone', ApJ 378, 413, 1991), but the ring rests on MSFC's 70%, which was read.

claims.claim: Random-walk path from the centre out to the 0.7 R ring, with short side-stubs
claims.note: MS92 models the transport as a random walk from the centre to the inner edge of the convective zone; MSFC: photons 'bounce from particle to particle through the radiative zone'. The 0.09 cm step cannot be drawn; the segment is under the 'not to scale' label (tag 100,000+ YEARS).

claims.claim: Path colour runs violet to pale yellow by log temperature from 15 MK (r=0), 7 MK (0.25 R), 2 MK (0.7 R), 5,700 K (surface): ~10% of the way to yellow at 0.25 R, ~26% at 0.7 R
claims.note: MSFC: centre about 15,000,000 C; at the core's edge 'only half its central value'; radiative zone falls 'from 7,000,000 C to about 2,000,000 C'; surface 5,700 K. Recomputed: log-T fraction 0.097 at 7 MK and 0.256 at 2 MK, matching 10% and 26%. The map stays far from yellow until the surface, so it does not suggest visible light inside. Hue is schematic (said in SOURCES).

claims.claim: Rotating dashed circles (convection cells) fill the shell between 0.7 R and the surface
claims.note: MSFC: convection zone is the outermost 30%; 'These convective motions carry heat quite rapidly to the surface', visible as granules and supergranules.

claims.claim: A fan of five short yellow light rays leaves the surface
claims.source_checked: NASA MSFC 'The Solar Interior'; NASA SVS 11084
claims.note: MSFC: the energy 'ultimately leaves the surface as visible light'; SVS: photons stream out from the surface.
